Hi @kozuechan

I have attempted this puzzle before but got caught in other stuff. I have now finished it and solved it fully. This is a good puzzle that reintroduced me to Hamiltonian paths, warnsdorff-style heuristics, and graph coloring. Warnsdorff was producing excellent Hamiltonian paths, but often closing them beside the start. Even-sized boards allowed structurally valid hamiltonian paths, while odd sized boards and problematic starting positions required carefully limited revisits. Large 19×19 and 20×20 cases are completing in roughly 12–14 seconds, one 19×19 validator (start=(9,11)) landed on an unlucky deterministic search sequence and timed out which with seed/path ordering tune was fixed. In short, I do not believe bigger/more validators would help me 'learn' more, puzzle is in already great shape. I have also tested with n=50 and to be honest, I do not think it is necessary at all or would add any value, existing validators already cover the important structural, correctness and performance challenges thoroughly. I am personally well satisfied with its 'Very Hard' classiciation. I would approve this puzzle when you take it out of WIP status and I believe it is ready to be published. 

Good work.

To solve an Expert / Very Hard puzzle involving both Palindromes and Pathfinding on grid systems (often mimicking advanced graph traversal on string states or grid coordinates where paths must form palindromic sequences), we can utilize a Bi-Directional Breadth-First Search (BFS) or a State-Space Graph Search.Core Problem ConceptIn advanced palindromic pathfinding puzzles, you are typically given a grid filled with letters and two coordinates: a start cell \(A\) and an end cell \(B\). Your objective is to find the shortest path from \(A\) to \(B\) such that the sequence of characters collected along the path forms a palindrome (reads the same forwards and backwards).A naive BFS exploring paths from \(A\) to \(B\) will time out because it must track the entire accumulated string state to verify if it forms a palindrome, causing an exponential state explosion.The Optimal Strategy: Simultaneous Bi-Directional ExpansionSince a palindrome is symmetrical from both ends, the most efficient solution is to step inward from both endpoints simultaneously. Instead of tracking individual paths, your search state tracks a pair of positions: (posA, posB).State Definition: A state is defined by a tuple (r1, c1, r2, c2), where (r1, c1) is the current cell expanding from the start, and (r2, c2) is the current cell expanding backwards from the destination.Matching Rule: We can transition from state (A, B) to a new neighbor state (A', B') if and only if the character at grid cell A' matches the character at grid cell B'.Termination (The Center of the Palindrome):For odd-length palindromes, the search succeeds when both paths meet at the exact same cell (r1 == r2 && c1 == c2).For even-length palindromes, the search succeeds when both paths cross over into adjacent, valid neighboring cells.This shrinks the state space from exponential down to \(\mathcal{O}((R \times C)^2)\), which computes instantly.

* My solution combines several algorithms, including a technique that is rarely (if ever) seen on CodinGame.
* The test cases are designed so that the puzzle cannot be solved without a deep understanding of the constraints.
* Proving that the solution produces valid output for all valid inputs is much harder than coding the solution. I expect many users will rely on trial and error rather than a rigorous proof.

This is an interesting puzzle, quite different from the types usually seen on CG.

Also, you did an excellent job on your first attempt at creating a puzzle using the CG SDK! I did't find any issues with the implementation itself. The points below are for improvement rather than bug reports.

Viewer
* I'm not sure whether the viewer animation should leave a trail as it moves along the path. That should make the path clearer, but in any case, it'll probably become difficult to see without zooming in when N grows larger.

Cases
* There aren't any cases where N is a 2-digit odd number. Please add a pair or two.

* For N ≥ 20, the starting points are consistently very close to the grid edges. Could some of them be positioned further inside?

* None of the visible tests use starting points on the left or right edges. Please update at least one test to include such a scenario. For reference, here's a summary of existing edge/corner starting points:

  • Corners: N=4 (Test & Validator), N=30 (Validator)

  • Left/right edges: N=6 (Validator)

  • Top/bottom edges: N=10 (Test), N=50 (Validator)
  
* From the summary, it appears that N is always even when the starting point is on an edge or at a corner. Would it be possible to include cases with odd N as well?

Thanks.

Statement

Constraints

Thank you again for your detailed feedback.

Goal
* I have added "Note that not every cell in the grid must be used (as shown in Example 2).".

Example 2
* I have specified the palindrome formed.
* Regarding the path clarity, one purpose of Example 2 is to implicitly demonstrate that the puzzle is solvable using a limited character set. Since players can set the language to PHP and copy-paste the grid to observe the behavior, I don't believe the clarity of the text grid is a major concern.

Constraints
* The limit was indeed chosen based on my Python solution. There are two primary worst case scenarios for execution time. I measured the performance using time.perf_counter in the CodinGame IDE over 10 runs for each case. The results are:

Worst Case 1: min = 3944ms, avg = 8207ms, max = 17931ms
Worst Case 2: min = 4487ms, avg = 9930ms, max = 18115ms

I have set the time limit to 25 seconds to be lenient. I have chosen not to reduce N as it might allow simpler C++ solutions to pass easily.

Cases
* Three pairs (N=5, 7, 19) of them are intentional edge cases that should remain.
* While the other two (N=9, 15) could be adjusted, I'm not sure if it's necessary. I'll keep them as is for now.
